1.1: 1.1 The Corinthians are Achaeans, and they likewise heard the word of truth from the Apostle, and were turned aside in many ways by false apostles. Some were led astray by the wordy eloquence of philosophy, others by the sect of the Jewish law. The Apostle calls them back to the true faith and the Gospel wisdom, writing to them from Ephesus through Timothy his disciple. Paul called. That is, called Apostle of Jesus Christ by all, by the privilege of the name. Here he does not call himself a servant, because there was more need of authority and commendation against the pride of the Corinthians, among whom he had been held cheap. And Sosthenes. Note that through the one who lived among them he hints that he had learned of their faults. Brother. By this he removes the suspicion that Sosthenes had reported them with ill intent, and shows it was from charity and the desire of correction.
1.2: 1.2 With all. He writes also to all the Corinthians who were their fellows, who laboured under the same vices.
1.3: 1.3 Grace. He first sets out the good things, so that others may be conformed to them. And the Lord Jesus Christ. Who is distinct from the Father in personal property, but is God, one with him in unity of substance.
1.5: 1.5 In all things. He supposes some part in every word, that is, in every kind of tongue, or in every manner of preaching, that is, for the lesser, the middling, and the perfect.
1.10: 1.10 I beseech. Up to this point he has praised the good. Having praised them, he invites the others to become like them.
1.11: 1.11 Chloe's. It is the name of a place or of a person. To some it seems to be a place, as if it were said: by those who are of Antioch. To others it seems to have been a woman devoted to God, with whom many were worshipping God.
1.12: 1.12 Now I mean this. Here he begins to act against those who boasted of their baptizers. I indeed. He marks the false apostles under his own name and the apostles', so that if he said, "in the name of this man or that," he might not seem to envy them and to wish to claim something for himself. Or he put the names of good apostles in order to show that if there is no boasting in the name of greater men, there is still less boasting in the name of those whose teaching is wicked.
1.13: 1.13 Is Christ divided? As if to say: you make many Christs, that is, givers of graces. Or: he who works the same in all is divided, while he is believed to work more in this one and less in that. Or because you say this, Christ is now divided by you, that is, separated. Was Paul crucified? By this he makes them blush at their falsehoods through a truth the Corinthians held, as through the resurrection of Christ, which they believed, he proves the resurrection of the dead, which they denied.
1.14: 1.14 I thank God, etc. AUGUSTINE. Paul gives thanks to God that he baptized none of them, because they, as if forgetting in whose name they were baptized, divided themselves by the names of men. For since baptism is of as much worth when given through a contemptible man as through the Apostle, it is known to be not his but Christ's, etc.
1.17: 1.17 But to preach the gospel. Even the less learned can baptize perfectly, but to preach the gospel perfectly is far harder and a rarer work. So the teacher of the Gentiles, more excellent than many, says he was sent to preach the gospel, not to baptize. Yet at times, when necessity pressed, he did this. Not in wisdom. Against the wisdom of the world. Not in wisdom of speech. He means the wisdom of the philosophers, which is so called though it is not wisdom; yet it is the kind that makes men wordy, by which the cross, that is the death of Christ, is emptied of force, and it is judged impossible, according to nature, that an immortal God should die. Of speech. Where the arrangement of words is sought, truth does not commend itself by its own power.
1.18: 1.18 To those who perish. That is, to the wise of the world, whose wisdom perishes and is shown to be false, and who are themselves to be condemned. The power of God. When, slain, he conquered the devil and freed man; or he gives the believers a power by which miracles are worked when the need requires.
1.19: 1.19 For it is written. Therefore he did not send me in wisdom, because he had foretold that he would not receive it in the gospel preaching, but would destroy and reject it from the company of his preachers; and so it came about.
1.21: 1.21 It pleased God, through the foolishness of the preaching, to save those who believe. That is, eternity comes to mortals through faith in the cross, so that salvation may be found where foolishness is believed.
1.26: 1.26 For see. What is truly foolish and weak in God is wiser and stronger than men. You can learn this by experience in yourselves. For the foolish and weak called you; such callers are counted among the foolish and weak things of God, and yet they confound the wise and strong. And they are truly such, because not many. He does not say, none, perhaps with himself in mind, who alone among the apostles was skilled in worldly letters, rich in earthly wealth, and distinguished by Roman dignity of birth; yet he counted these as nothing and did not use them.
1.27: 1.27 But the foolish things. See, they openly act against God's ordinance, because they boast of the wisdom of the world, when God sets forth humility. For God came humble, seeking the humble, not the lofty. Though he first chose the poor, the unlearned, the weak, he does not abandon the wise, the rich, the noble; but if he had chosen these first, they would rightly have thought they were chosen for such things, and so there would be in them the pride by which man fell. Unless the fisherman had gone first in faith, the humble would not have been followed by the orator. Hence the learned Nathanael was not chosen as an apostle.
1.29: 1.29 That no one may boast. Of himself, but of God, as is shown there: let him who boasts, boast in the Lord.
1.30: 1.30 But of him. Let no one boast of himself, yet there is another glory, because you are of him.
2.2: 2.2 For I judged not. He who speaks higher things to one less able to receive them is not serving their profit but showing himself off.
2.6: 2.6 The perfect. Not the knowers and teachers, who do not need it, but hearers who are now capable.
2.7: 2.7 In a mystery. By expounding the mysteries of the Old Testament in which Christ was signified, as in the offering of Abel or of Abraham. Which was hidden. Because it is not in words but in power: not comprehended by human reason, but believed by the efficacy of the Spirit.
2.8: 2.8 For if they had known. Whether the lesser knew him to be the Messiah promised in the law, or the greater knew him to be God or the Son of God, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.
2.9: 2.9 Nor has it entered the heart of man. What enters the heart is below the heart; what is above the heart is the eternal thing to which the heart ascends. Or it is not man, but the Spirit who knows. It entered. A thing is said to go up into the heart when, well understood, it pleases.
2.10: 2.10 Searches, etc. The Spirit of God is said to search all things, not to find out what he does not know, but because he leaves nothing at all that he does not know, or because he makes you search. For what you do by his gift, he is said to do, because without him you would not do it.
2.12: 2.12 But the Spirit who is of God. The Holy Spirit is certainly of the Father and the Son, and also ours. For what has been given is referred both to the one who gave and to those to whom he gave. So the Holy Spirit is not only of the Father and the Son who gave him, but also ours who received him. And this is not that spirit of ours in which we exist; for the spirit of ours in which we exist is the spirit of man, which is in him. Yet we have received even that spirit which is of man. But it is one thing that we received that we might be, another that we received that we might be holy. The spirit of man is taken in Scripture for the soul itself or for the rational power of the soul. For he gave us nature that we might be, soul that we might live, mind that we might understand. That we may know. Many have the gifts of God, and not knowing from whom they have them, are puffed up with ungodly vanity. No one is blessed by the gifts of God who is ungrateful to the giver; hence in the Gospel: to him who has, it shall be given. To have fully is to know whence one has. He therefore who does not have, that is, who does not know whence he has, even what he has shall be taken from him, Luke 8.
2.13: 2.13 Spiritual things. Which you Corinthians are not; and therefore it is your fault, not ours, that we have not spoken of greater things.
2.14: 2.14 But the animal man. The animal man is so called by his life: he who is carried along by the dissolute wantonness of his soul, which the ruling spirit does not hold within the bounds of the natural order, because he does not submit himself to be ruled by God. By the sense of the mind he is called animal who judges God by bodily imaginings, or the letter of the law, or philosophical reason. Because it is judged spiritually. The animal man cannot understand spiritual things, because they are examined; that is, the examination and approval of those spiritual things is made only spiritually, that is by the spiritual man; and the word is read in a personal sense: is examined. Or thus: the animal man does not understand spiritual things, because it is spiritually, that is through spiritual things alone, that it is proved that he is animal; for he rejects what he hears, and they are set before him for no other reason than that he may be examined.
2.15: 2.15 But the spiritual man. He is such either in life or in knowledge. Spiritual in life is he who, having the Spirit of the Lord as ruler, governs his soul; spiritual in knowledge is he who, though he sees in part and through a mirror, yet does not judge of God according to images of bodies, or the letter of the law, or human philosophy, but being subject to the Spirit of God judges most surely and faithfully. All things. Not indeed everything that divine knowledge contains, but what suffices for righteousness and life, that is, all things that are to be judged.
3.2: 3.2 For you are still carnal. He rebukes those who complained that they had not long ago heard spiritual things, when they were still unworthy to hear them. His ministers. AUGUSTINE. Man ministers outwardly as a servant, etc., down to because God works the willing and the doing.
3.8: 3.8 Are one. It might seem that although they give nothing from themselves, God yet works more through this one than through that.
3.9: 3.9 Helpers. In tilling the Lord's field; not corrupters, as some say. This is clear from the fact that you are God's husbandry. Husbandry. Because he cultivates you for fruit. Building, because he who cultivates dwells in you. And so field and building are the same, which is not so in visible things. We cultivate God by adoring, not by adorning. But he so cultivates us that he makes us better.
3.11: 3.11 For the foundation. AUGUSTINE, in the book On Faith and Works, chapter 15. The faith of Christian grace, that is, the faith which works through love, etc., down to of which it is written: The furnace tests the potter's vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests men, Ecclesiasticus 27. Christ. That is, the faith of Christ, which works through love, through which Christ dwells in hearts. No other is the foundation. And this lets no one perish.
3.12: 3.12 But if anyone. In gold, silver, and precious stones, excellent teaching is signified; in the other three, vain teaching, which if it deceives now will be seen in the fire, because it will burn while the good remains, and the reward of the good, that is of the good teaching, will be eternal life. Wood, hay, stubble. These are not to be taken of evil works, as if faith without works could save, which is not so. AUGUSTINE, on Psalm 30. Let no one who has wicked works promise himself the kingdom of God, etc., down to the smallest and lightest sins, which fire easily consumes.
3.13: 3.13 For the day. Here the day is the day of man acting at his own will; but in the judgment or at the death of each, it is the day of the Lord, judging according to merits. Indeed, the judgment even here begins from the house of God, that is, the punishment begins with those who are to be saved, and will be completed in the reprobate. For the elect are punished that they may not be punished there. In which day is the fire of tribulation by which the love of temporal things is burned, when they are saddened over what is lost, whence it is said: Such will have tribulation of the flesh. But the fire of the last judgment will last until those who are to be saved are purified. The fire will test. We read of two fires to come. One eternal, by which the reprobate will be punished forever, which will follow the judgment. The other will precede it, by which the face of this world will be burned up and will amend those who have built on wood, hay, stubble. But those who built gold, silver, precious stones are safe from both fires.
3.14: 3.14 Reward. Not only after the end, but even in this life he has the rest of his soul that despises all things.
3.16: 3.16 Do you not know, etc. He puts this first to prick those who live shamefully and defile their bodies, especially the one who has his father's wife. Here he treats of those who build upon the foundation.
3.17: 3.17 But if anyone. That man will be saved, but through fire; yet if anyone will destroy the temple which you are, God will destroy him. And you do not know this. Temple. AUGUSTINE. Those in whom God dwells by faith are the temple of God, etc., as even now the angels of God are a temple. AUGUSTINE. Such a gathering is the building of the temple of God; such a gathering is made not by carnal generation but by spiritual regeneration. God therefore dwells in each, as in his temples, and in all gathered together, as in his temple. God is therefore present everywhere, and present everywhere whole, not dwelling everywhere but in his temple, to which he is kind and favorable by grace. Yet he is received by some more fully, by others less. And he dwells in animal men and little ones, not by age of the flesh but of the mind, because in them he works secretly that they may be his temple, and this he perfects in those who make progress and persevere in making progress. THE SAME. But someone might say: before God made heaven and earth, before, etc., down to and those are most blessed to whom this is to have God, that is, to know him. For the wisdom of this world, etc. AMBROSE. Wisdom is wrongly put for cunning.
3.21: 3.21 Let no one, etc. Take pride in the baptizers or teachers. No one. Because they are yours; because all things are given to serve you, and one should not boast except in more excellent things. In men. Because they are not givers of graces, whether they are good or bad, but only ministers.
3.22: 3.22 For all things. Let them not each defend teachers or baptizers for themselves, when they use all of them. The world is ours if we set its course in the will of God. The present life is ours if it is lived modestly and for the glory of God. Death is ours if we gladly die for Christ in hope of the future. The present is ours if we so use it that we do not offend. The future, if we, believing in it, desire it more. Whether life, etc. Both the life and death of teachers should be for the edification of their subjects. Or by life, understand holy men and angels, who strive for the progress of the faithful; by death, the devil and his members, who in persecuting serve the good of the servants of God.
3.23: 3.23 And you are Christ's. So that as these things are subject to us, so we may be subject to Christ. And Christ is God's. His own Son doing his will, that we also may do his. Why then, to the wrong of Christ, do you hope for something from men?
4.1: 4.1 Let a man so regard us. So far he has spoken of the boasting of the false apostles; here he treats of his own contempt. Let a man so regard us. The Apostle says this because they thought less of him; but let a man think as God who chose him thinks. And stewards. AUGUSTINE. Not only good but also bad are stewards, etc., down to it is to be a partaker of him.
4.2: 4.2 Here it is now required. So we are to be judged, but here among you, which is not so elsewhere. Now in the present, when we ought to wait until God judges.
4.3: 4.3 Myself. It is dangerous for you to judge of the unknown things of my heart or of others'. For such a depth must be believed to be in man that it is hidden even from the man in whom it is, as the depth of weakness lay hidden in Peter when he rashly promised to die with the Lord. Since then each one can pass a true sentence on himself either not at all or hardly, how can he judge another, when no one knows what is done in man except the spirit of man? By a human. That is, by men, while it is their day, and it is not the day of the Lord. Human. Because there is a day of the Lord, on which he will judge, when each will give an account for himself, and then the secrets of hearts will be laid open.
4.4: 4.4 For I am not conscious of anything. AMBROSE. Do not say: we have not sinned. Holy Paul said: Though I am conscious of nothing against myself; but he added, yet I am not justified by this. And you also, if you are conscious of nothing, still confess to the Lord, lest something escape you.
4.5: 4.5 Until the Lord comes. Otherwise a wrong is done to the judge, because it is a wrong to the judge if the sentence goes forth from the servant before his own judgment. He will bring to light. That is, he will make open the hidden things of darkness, that is, of sins. Then each will have praise. For the one who acts or thinks well; but here it is not known who is worthy of praise.
4.6: 4.6 These things, and Apollos. I have set forth a figure for all, that all may shrink from it as from us. That not, etc., one, etc. From that one, that is, a better than he, that is, as though there were another besides him who is nothing, as far as concerns himself or his ministry.
4.7: 4.7 For who makes you different? From the mass of the lost? No one but God. Or if you were baptized by Peter, how are you distinguished from him who was baptized by Paul? That one has nothing from the baptizer, nor have you. Or he rebukes those same who boasted of the teaching of the false apostles. As if to say: You boast on their behalf, but what do you have from them that you did not have from me? And if from me, why do you boast against me, as if you had not received the same from me? And what, etc. He tries to remove another kind of arrogance, namely that a man should not be proud on account of some grace given him by God, thinking he has it from himself or from a minister. But if you received it. He says this against those who, hearing the same things from the Apostle, boasted of the teaching of the false apostles, who by eloquence commending themselves turned the glory to themselves; while the Apostle had made himself seem contemptible that he might give glory to God. So the Apostle speaks to them ironically, as if granting what they thought of themselves, when he adds.
4.8: 4.8 Already you are filled. As if: I ask you, Why do you boast? etc.; but I seem not to do this rightly; for you are already filled, already rich, which is irony, as if he said: It is not so. For these are the words of one angry, not of one affirming. You reign. To reign truly is to be secure in the hope and promises of God, and to rejoice in adversity.
4.9: 4.9 For I think. As if to say: By no means is it to be thought so. He speaks ironically. I say without us, because through the evils we suffer, God shows us the last of the apostles, of whom no care is taken, as men appointed to death, that is, for no use, but kept for death; which is seen from this, that men gather to our spectacle as to a monster; by which we are the more proved to be friends of God. Or therefore you ought to reign with us, because I think and am certain that we are like the last days of Elijah and Enoch in tribulations. And to angels. Good angels and good men praise, the wicked mock: these are the right hand and the left. We use these to strike the enemy, that is, the devil; neither do those lift us up, nor these break us.
4.10: 4.10 For Christ's sake. Whose cross we preach, which you, keeping silent, seem to be prudent in Christ.
4.13: 4.13 As the refuse. Through all these things we are proved in Christ to be prudent and strong.
4.14: 4.14 Not to shame you. He softens harsh things with gentle ones, like a healing physician.
4.15: 4.15 Tutors. By naming tutors he signifies boys. Through the gospel. He added through the gospel, lest what is God's be thought to be his own. For the Lord says in the Gospel: Call no one your father on earth, for one is your Father, God, Matthew 23; not that this name be taken from others, but that the grace of God by which we are begotten into eternal life be not ascribed to the nature or power or even the holiness of any man.
4.19: 4.19 If the Lord wills. He says this to show that if he did not go, it was God's not willing, because of their unworthiness.
4.20: 4.20 In power. He brings words of terror so that the puffed-up may be humbled and prepare to receive him. Far be it that dutiful sons should say: If you are coming with a rod, do not come. For it is better to be instructed by the father's rod than to perish in the flattery of a plunderer.
5.1: 5.1 It is actually reported. He begins to treat of fornication, and rebukes that fornicator who had his father's wife, and those who tolerated him. For they too were sharers, since they allowed the guilty man of so great a sin to meet with them uncorrected. So he showed that not only that man was guilty of death, but also those who clung to him were not free from the crime.
5.2: 5.2 You are puffed up. With the wind of pride, which drives out mercy; for if one member suffers, the others suffer with it.
5.4: 5.4 In the name of the Lord. In this way I have judged: that you, gathered together without any dissension (with whom my authority and the power of Christ will work), deliver such a one to Satan.
5.5: 5.5 To deliver, etc. The Apostle is said to have had this power, that when he could not remove someone from folly he might hand him to the devil to be vexed, until, professing penance, he gave up the evil. That the spirit may be saved. So the Apostle delivers to Satan not cruelly but lovingly. So Moses judged a few of the worshipers of idols, terrifying them for the present and establishing discipline for the future. So also Elijah and other good men: because thus fear is struck into others, and the sin is lessened in the sinners themselves. Hence Christ did not reprove this example of Elijah in his disciples; but because from hatred and not from love of correction they desired the vengeance of fire on those who did not give them hospitality; so also Peter is read to have avenged himself on Ananias and his wife, or he delivers, that the Holy Spirit, by whom the defiled are laid bare, may be saved for them, not lost on the day of judgment.
5.6: 5.6 The whole lump. They were participants, while they tolerated the guilty man. But if one has not the power to cast out the one he knows guilty, or is not able to prove it, he is free of blame. And it is not for a judge to condemn without an accuser, as Christ did not cast out Judas.
5.7: 5.7 Dough. It is flour bound together by water without leaven, that is, unleavened. He wills therefore that they be one thing through love, pure from the corruption of sin, clothed with the new man as they were made in baptism. Zyma is Greek, fermentum Latin. Pascha is an immolation, not a passage, as some think; for first Pascha and then passage: because first is the example of the Savior, and so salvation. AUGUSTINE. This renewal of our life is a certain passage from death to life, etc., down to for Christ our Pasch has been sacrificed.
5.8: 5.8 Of sincerity. Of new life and truth, without any fraud, so that sincerity makes the life clean, and truth excludes all fraud.
5.10: 5.10 Otherwise, etc. Such could not be gained for Christ if one avoided their company and table; hence the Lord also ate with publicans and sinners.
5.11: 5.11 But now. Then I wrote to you, and you did not take it well, but now I write definitely. Named. The Apostle wished that naming to be understood which is brought against someone with a sentence, in judicial order, and with integrity. For if any naming at all sufficed, many innocent would be condemned, because crimes are often falsely named against someone. By saying named he shows sufficiently that the wicked are to be removed from the communion of the Church not rashly or in any way, but by judgment, or if they cannot be removed by judgment, they should rather be tolerated, lest anyone, perversely avoiding the wicked and leaving the Church, send to hell those whom he seems to flee.
6.1: 6.1 Does anyone dare. On the occasion of this judgment he begins to treat of lawsuits, in which the Corinthians sinned in many ways, for instance, that scorning the faithful they went to unbelieving judges, or appointed foolish judges, and quarreled, and defrauded, and did other such things.
6.2: 6.2 That. Because by the example of their faith, unbelief of this kind will be condemned.
6.4: 6.4 Secular judgments therefore. Because the Apostle had said that they could judge these least matters, he determines who should be appointed to settle such affairs, namely the contemptible who are in the Church. For the greater ought to attend to spiritual things. AUGUSTINE, in the book On the Work of Monks, chapter 20. The wise therefore who were among the faithful in the places, etc., down to or by intervening to cut them short.
6.5: 6.5 To your shame. Let those who have perceived the wisdom of outward things examine earthly cases. But those endowed with spiritual gifts ought not to be entangled in earthly business; that, while not compelled to dispose lower goods, they may be able to serve higher goods. Yet care must be taken that those who shine with spiritual gifts do not wholly abandon the affairs of weak neighbors, but either commit them to others to whom it is fitting to handle them, or manage them themselves.
6.8: 6.8 Brothers. Whom you ought to help, and so you lose the kingdom, and worse, because you know.
6.9: 6.9 Do you not know. Note that he repeats so often, You do not know; as if: In following me, you ought to know this; but following the false apostles, you have become foolish.
6.11: 6.11 But you were sanctified. Note that the repeated conjunction but gives no small weight to the sentence.
6.12: 6.12 All things are lawful for me. Because he said it is better to bear wrong than to go to law badly, lest anyone think his own goods should in no way be reclaimed, he adds: It is lawful for me to reclaim all that is mine, yet I will not reclaim it, because not all things are expedient for my course, but they hinder. Again by another cause he shows the same. As if: They are lawful, but I will not reclaim them, because being free, I do not wish to be brought under the power of a judge; or, I do not wish to be under the dominion of any thing, so as to offend a brother on its account.
6.13: 6.13 Food for the belly. Because of these things they are not to be reclaimed, yet food is owed to the belly. By these things note what is necessary to nature, and therefore it is lawful to reclaim them. But we are not to labor much for them, because they will be destroyed, and therefore it is lawful that judgment be made of them or be passed over.
6.15: 6.15 Bodies. The body cannot but be holy which the sanctified Spirit uses. Are members, etc. As all the members governed by one and the same soul are one body, so all who are given life by the same Holy Spirit are made one body in Christ. Of Christ. Because he took a body and is the head of bodies.
6.16: 6.16 One body. The natural philosophers hold that they are so united that if their blood were mingled it would be wholly joined.
6.17: 6.17 But he who cleaves, etc. Not by identity of substance but by participation, when the one coming by faith so cleaves to him as to share in his blessedness, which will then be full when his desire is satisfied with unchangeable goods, namely in the Trinity itself, his Lord, whose image he is.
6.18: 6.18 Flee fornication. With other vices one may wait for the conflict, but flee this, do not approach, because it cannot be better conquered in any other way. For every sin. No sin so dishonors and defiles the body as that. But he who fornicates. This is not said on account of the quantity of fornication, as though it alone were in the body and the others outside the body. For many sins are as great as fornication, or greater. But on account of its quality, because it defiles the body more foully than other sins.
6.19: 6.19 Temple. From this it is clear that the Holy Spirit is God; for if he were not God, he would surely not have ourselves as a temple. Not only the Holy Spirit, but also the Father and the Son have us as a temple. The temple of God, that is of the whole Trinity, is therefore the holy Church.
6.20: 6.20 And carry God. To carry God is to show the image of God in well-done works. In your body. If you do not spare yourself for your own sake, spare yourself for God's, who made you his house. If you overturn it, you sin against God, which is a grave kind of sin; but to sin against man is another kind.
7.1: 7.1 Concerning what. On the occasion of the fornication which he forbids, he goes on to marriage, about which they had asked. And he treats it in three ways: according to counsel, according to indulgence, according to precept.
7.7: 7.7 Each one, etc. No one should be constrained, lest, forbidden what is lawful, he fall into the unlawful, but let him himself choose what to follow, though it is better to be more inclined to this.
7.9: 7.9 To burn is to be driven or overcome by desires. He does not therefore say better as though it were good to burn and better to marry, but he followed the custom of speech.
7.11: 7.11 But if she departs. It is one thing to depart, another to abstain by common consent. For the former is evil, the latter good. AMBROSE. He does not add about the husband as he does about the woman, because it is lawful for the husband to take another, because the inferior does not wholly use this law, because the superior, which is said by forgers to have been added. And let the husband not. A husband ought not to put away his wife, because he would make her commit adultery. But if she is an adulteress he does not make her so, but sends away an adulteress. The cause which Christ excepted is here passed over in silence, because it is well known, namely fornication.
7.12: 7.12 For to the rest. Where both are faithful, the Apostle gave this command of the Lord. For to the rest, where both are not faithful (which happened at the beginning of the Church, when the Gospel began to be preached), I say, etc. If any brother, etc. Idolatry and any harmful superstition is fornication, and the Lord for the cause of fornication permitted a wife to be put away, but did not command it, and so he gave the Apostle room to advise that whoever wishes should not put away an unbelieving spouse, by whom perhaps he might become faithful.
7.14: 7.14 Is sanctified. Because this often happens, that one is converted to the faith through the other. Or the unbelieving husband is clean as regards the faithful wife, and the faithful wife suffers no uncleanness from union with him. Otherwise. If you put each other away, unwilling to live together, and join yourselves to others, you are adulterers, and your children are illegitimate and therefore unclean; now they are holy, because born of lawful marriages, and born under veneration of the Creator.
7.15: 7.15 For not. It is not a marriage merely that is without devotion to God: and therefore there is no sin in one who puts away for God's sake if he has joined himself to another. But if both believe, the marriage is confirmed by knowledge of God. In peace. One should not quarrel with the one who departs, because he departs out of hatred of God.
7.16: 7.16 For how do you know. He exhorted above by the things that happened; now because the same can happen, he exhorts to the same. These things are done not by the command of law but by free charity.
7.17: 7.17 The Lord has distributed. God gave to each the time when he is to be saved, that is, he knows when he will believe, and waits until he believes; so you too wait.
7.18: 7.18 Was anyone circumcised. The Apostle nowhere takes away a custom which, kept, does not hinder salvation, warning only that the hope of salvation not be placed in such things, since they are kept only on account of the offense of the weak. Hence he says they are nothing, adding: Circumcision is nothing.
7.20: 7.20 Let each in that. This regards those conditions or customs of life which do no harm to faith and good morals. For as the married person, so the robber also is called to the faith of Christ. But the one in marriage, not from marriage. The other not in robbery, but from robbery. For it is not necessary that spouses cease to be spouses on account of the faith of Christ, as it is necessary that robbers cease to be robbers.
7.21: 7.21 A slave, etc. Above he gave one example of manner of living, here another of condition of office. Rather use it. Because the more anyone is despised in this world for God's sake, the more he will be exalted in the future.
7.22: 7.22 A freedman. Because rescued from sins, which make slaves. Therefore let not the slave be despised for his condition, nor the freedman, rescued, being lifted up, set himself above the slave.
7.23: 7.23 You were bought. Return the favor, that you be servants of Christ, not of men. These are servants of men who subject themselves to human superstitions. Servants of men. Which happens to you if you say: I am of Paul, I of Apollos, etc.
7.25: 7.25 Concerning virgins. Because of that fornicator, he teaches about avoiding all fornication.
7.26: 7.26 Necessity, he says, meaning the hardship of the age which married people often suffer. To the weak he offers a weak reason. For he could have made the reason for virginity worthier by further commending its gift. For virginity goes beyond the condition of human nature, by which men are made like angels. Yet the victory of virgins is greater than that of angels. For angels live without flesh, but virgins triumph in the flesh.
7.29: 7.29 This therefore I say. Here he warns to temperance, as if to say: When you are joined, let it be done without sin; this counsel I give you, that those who have may be as though not having. This he does who, having a wife, renders the debt and does not demand it; who on account of his own weakness takes a wife, grieving rather that he could not be without a wife than rejoicing that he took one, and especially because by equal consent they keep continence. Those marriages are certainly to be judged more blessed which, whether children were begotten or offspring scorned, were able to keep continence by equal consent.
7.34: 7.34 She thinks, etc. For she, not fearing damnation and secure about salvation, thinks only of the things of the Lord. That she may be holy, etc. This applies to the married woman too, but more to the unmarried, who, free from worldly necessities by which the married woman is bound, gives herself more intensely to heavenly precepts.
7.35: 7.35 Not to cast a snare. But tending to that, I say what is honorable, that a man be chaste in body and mind, not that marriage is shameful, but that this is more honorable and has the facility of praying to God.
7.36: 7.36 But if anyone, etc. As he has determined about virgins, so he determines about guardians.
7.38: 7.38 He does better. Because before God he lays up merit for her, and frees her from worldly anxiety. And therefore he rightly says: It is better what is lawful and expedient than what is lawful and not expedient.
7.39: 7.39 A woman is bound. He had said that a woman departing from her husband for fornication should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband, and he had not said whether she should remain so for her whole life or for the husband's lifetime; this he therefore determines. So a virgin can always marry whom she wishes, but a woman, that is a married one, even sent away for fornication and separated from her husband, is bound by the law while her husband lives, etc. But if he sleeps. He does not say first, or second, or how many; for we are not to define what the Apostle does not define: hence I ought not to condemn any marriage, nor bring shame on them by their number. The Lord does not condemn the woman of seven husbands, nor does he say she cannot be so in the resurrection. He says only: they neither marry nor are given in marriage. So I dare not, against the sense of human modesty, say that they may marry as often as they wish, nor from my own heart condemn any marriages. What is said of the wife of one husband applies to every widow.
7.40: 7.40 More blessed, etc. He shows enough that a faithful woman remarrying after her husband's death is blessed, but more blessed if she does not marry. But I think. The Apostle does not doubt, but rebukes the scorners, as the Lord also, saying: If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also; or, Do you think he will find faith on earth? By a word of doubt he reproves unbelief.
8.1: 8.1 Concerning these. As if to say: you know as well as I that it is lawful to eat them; because we all have knowledge. He says this of those who, having knowledge, ate with offense. These he first rebukes, and says they do not know sufficiently. Others, being ignorant, ate under veneration of the idol. Knowledge puffs up. Of itself knowledge is useless, but with charity it is useful. Of itself it puffs up into pride, like the demons, who are named by a Greek name from knowledge. To restrain the elation of knowledge a thorn was given to Paul. It is better to know our own weakness than the natures of things; he who adds this knowledge adds the sorrow of exile from desire for the homeland.
8.3: 8.3 But if anyone loves God. He loves God who for charity's sake tempers his knowledge, that it may profit his brother for whom Christ died.
8.4: 8.4 Concerning food. Having censured their knowledge, he at last reveals what the true one is. An idol is nothing in the world. That is, among the creatures of the world. For God formed the matter, but the folly of men gave the form. For whatever is among creatures was made through the Word. But the form of man in the idol was not made through the Word, as neither was sin made through the Word. But it is nothing, and men become nothing when they sin. Except one. He says this lest God be thought to be in the idol.
8.5: 8.5 For even if there are many gods. That is, among the Gentiles there are several: whom our God terrifies, that is, the demons, who, wishing to seem gods, demand for themselves what is due to the true God, altars, sacrifices, and the rest. But ours makes men gods.
8.6: 8.6 God. God is said in three ways. By substance, the Trinity is called God. By adoption, the saints who by the grace of adoption are gods. By name only, demons and idols. From whom. All things are from the Father, but created through the Son. Not some things through the Son, others through the Father, but the same; otherwise not all things would be through the Father, nor all through the Son; but if all through the Father and all through the Son, then the same things were made through the Father as through the Son; the Son is therefore equal to the Father, and the working of both is inseparable. And one. Of Christ he adds by reason of his humanity, but of the Holy Spirit it was not needful.
8.7: 8.7 Is defiled. Through those, namely, who have knowledge of one God but not with charity, by whom the weak were led into this error, whose conscience is defiled, not their food.
8.12: 8.12 Against Christ. To sin against Christ is to deny Christ.
9.1: 9.1 Am I not free? He begins to set himself forth as an example, that as he abstains from lawful things for the scandal of the brethren, so should they. As if he said: Abstain from this lawful thing, because I have the freedom to receive wages and yet I do not receive them. Even if it was introduced in this way, he intends nevertheless to prove himself an apostle, because on the occasion of the false apostles the Corinthians had thought less of him.
9.4: 9.4 Do we not, etc. BEDE. The Lord permitted, he did not command, etc., down to it is therefore a power, not a command of the Lord, to receive support. A sister, a woman. The Lord had women in his company, that they might not seem foreign to salvation, and they ministered to him; so also the apostles.
9.6: 9.6 Of working. The word of working is more honorable than that of receiving.
9.7: 9.7 Who serves as a soldier. Lest, because he abstains, he seem to have reproved his fellow apostles, he adds: Who serves as a soldier. CHRYSOSTOM. Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? By the former he shows dangers; by this, labor and much misery and care, and he adds a third example in these words. Who feeds, etc. THE SAME. He shows great diligence, and what is owed to the teacher by his subjects. This is clear from the following: for the apostles were soldiers, and farmers, and shepherds, not of wars, nor of land, nor of brute animals, but of souls endowed with reason, and of that army which is armed against demons. And of the milk. The milk of the flock is whatever is given by the people to those set over them.
9.8: 9.8 Do I say, etc., THE SAME. That is: Do I confirm my case by human examples only? Or does the law not say this also?
9.9: 9.9 Is it for oxen. They are indeed a care, but not so that he should make a law for them.
9.12: 9.12 Lest any offense. That is, lest it be said of us that we preach the gospel rather for gain and temporal profit than for the salvation of souls and eternal reward, and the Gospel be held as something for sale.
9.13: 9.13 Do you not know. He returns again to what he had begun, showing that it is lawful for him, and yet he does not do it. Natural reason also holds that one should live from where he labors.
9.15: 9.15 But I. The Apostle abstains from expenses, lest he be a pattern for the grasping false apostles. It is good, etc. Whoever is unwilling to use what is owed to him gives more to the Church. The Apostle therefore had the greatest glory before God, by not demanding wages from the weak, but earning his daily food by his own labors. Glory. Which I have before God, sympathizing with the weak.
9.16: 9.16 For even if, etc. For a reward: or, if I preach thus, I have no glory; because then it would be of necessity, because woe, that is, want, would be there as with the false apostles. Necessity, of sustaining this life. Woe. Because I have nothing to live on.
9.17: 9.17 For if willingly. Because the reward is from the will. Let us see how: namely if I do so out of love that I would rather suffer want than abuse my power. But if unwillingly. So that what I am compelled to by necessity benefits others but not me. A dispensation is entrusted to me. Here dispensation is understood so that, as a servant, he dispenses another's wealth, from which he himself takes nothing but food. Elsewhere a dispenser is one who, as a son, ministers the Gospel to his co-heirs. We ought not therefore to preach the gospel in order to eat, but to eat in order to preach; so that food is not the good that is sought but a necessary thing that is added.
9.19: 9.19 From all. From the businesses of men, receiving nothing from them; Of all, understand of men, I made myself a servant, supporting all, as a good steward supports the weak, most of all you, O Corinthians, by my patience. And I did this not by cunning craft but by the affection of one who suffers with them, that I might gain more for Christ.
9.20: 9.20 As a Jew. JEROME. Not truly a Jew, as not truly a Gentile, with whom in foods, etc., down to how he would wish to be served himself if he were sick.
9.21: 9.21 To those under the law, etc. The Samaritans, who receive the books of Moses, which the Jews do not use together with them. They are of the origin of the Persians, whom the king of the Assyrians or Persians, when Israel was removed, set to dwell in the places of Samaria.
9.22: 9.22 All things to all. He yielded to all, yet did not exceed religion.
9.24: 9.24 Do you not know, etc. He shows how great is the usefulness of our law, in which the palm is promised not to one but to all; and he who comes first waits to be crowned with the latecomer. Prize. It is the reward of the race.
9.25: 9.25 For everyone, etc. Many comparisons are drawn from things not to be praised, as in the Gospel about the unjust judge who would not hear the widow, and the lazy one who lent loaves not from friendship but out of weariness; so here athletic and playful things are not commended.
9.26: 9.26 Not as. He runs uncertainly who does such things that he can hope from some and despair from others.
9.27: 9.27 I chastise my body. The Apostle terrified us with his own fear. For what will the lamb do where the ram trembles? Lest perhaps, etc. Which could happen quickly; then others must the more beware lest by offending they be reprobate.
10.1: 10.1 For I do not wish. For one who wishes to understand, so it must be done; for baptism and the sacraments do not suffice, as some think; as neither did God's benefits avail the Jews, since afterward they sinned. That our fathers. By the example of the Jews, who offended by their negligence, he makes them careful. Under the cloud. Because all things happened to them in a figure of us.
10.2: 10.2 Baptized in Moses. They were cleansed under the leadership of Moses by those signs they saw. Or, they received a sign of baptism, which was of the same worth to believers. They were baptized, because freed from death and cleansed by it from the ignorance of God which weighed on all the Gentiles, and prepared to receive the law. Or they are called baptized because they bore the form of our sacrament. Moses signifies Christ, the cloud the Holy Spirit, the sea baptism.
10.3: 10.3 The same food. That is, by faith: different in time, different in kind. Spiritual. That is, signifying something spiritual. When he says spiritual, he shows that it is understood spiritually in Christ, and he hints this of all, and explains one: the rock was Christ.
10.4: 10.4 The rock following them. That is, satisfying their will, because wherever they went the overflowing waters followed; so Christ accompanies his own in the desert of this world. Or, following, that is, signifying the truth that was to follow. But the rock. A thing that is signified is usually named by the name of the thing that it signifies. The rock. That is Christ, was following, because where human help failed, he was present.
10.7: 10.7 Neither be idolaters, etc. He touches those who feasted in an idol temple, thinking themselves free from guilt. The people sat down. By recalling them he marks what is among the Corinthians, showing how gravely it was punished among the Jews. To play. That is, to worship, which is like the play of boys. For childhood is easy to play. And what is so like childish play as to worship idols?
10.9: 10.9 Neither let us tempt Christ. Note that Christ is God, whom the Jews tempted, and therefore they perished by serpents, until the bronze serpent was lifted up, and those who looked at it were healed of the bites.
10.10: 10.10 In a figure. See, he shows why those signs are no longer observed, since the matter is clear for our correction.
10.11: 10.11 They were written. Not only for our sake. For by these examples we are summoned to a more upright life, that we may deserve either a reward, if we are obedient, or a heavier punishment if disobedient. The ends of the ages. Because we are in the last age, and ought to be corrected the more by so many examples of those before. Or the ends of the age have come upon us, worldliness is ended in us; and therefore it is the more shameful if we sin.
10.12: 10.12 Let him take heed lest he fall. As those who, presuming on knowledge, ate food offered to idols to the scandal of their brothers, and boasting of the false apostles, judged the Apostle when they themselves were guilty.
10.13: 10.13 No temptation, etc. He urges that a human temptation take hold of them, not another. For it is a human temptation that, in need or pressure, a man should not despair of God by seeking human aid. To suffer for Christ, then, is a human temptation, by which one advances before God. That you may be able to bear. Which comes through humility. For he keeps the humble in every temptation, that they may not burst in the furnace who have no wind of pride.
10.14: 10.14 Wherefore, etc. Because the sacraments alone do not save, and because he who falls is punished, and because God's help is not lacking, flee the worship of idols. Or, let not the wise eat food offered to idols to the offense of the weak, to whom they would seem idolaters. Or, that the weak themselves not be idolaters, and I speak something lofty, as to the prudent, that you may flee; and therefore judge carefully. Or: now I speak to the weak, as above to the prudent.
10.16: 10.16 The cup of blessing. We must flee the worship of idols because, as one who eats food offered to idols is one with the demon, so through the body of Christ he is one with Christ. The bread which we break. BEDE. When Christ is eaten, life is eaten. But who would dare, etc., down to he remained whole with the Father, that he might feed the angels.
10.17: 10.17 For we, though many, etc. One bread by the union of faith, hope, and charity. A body by the service of charity: because we are one, and ought to be of one mind. He says this that one faith may have one mind and work.
10.18: 10.18 Consider. It is a comparison for understanding what was said above. He added, according to the flesh, because there is an Israel according to the Spirit, which no longer follows the old shadows but the truth that follows them (which was signified by those preceding shadows); and offers to God in the body of Christ a sacrifice of praise, since the God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting.
10.19: 10.19 What then? Because I said, flee the worship of idols, I seem to say that something offered to idols is something great, but I do not say this; rather I say that what the Gentiles sacrifice they sacrifice to demons: because in the idol the devil is worshiped, who is worse than the idol.
10.20: 10.20 To become partners with demons. AUGUSTINE, book II On Christian Doctrine, chapters 20, 21, etc. To this kind belong also consultations and pacts, etc., down to the mathematicians, who try to foretell the outcomes of actions, are so called.
10.22: 10.22 Or do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? They seem to be jealous of and to envy the Lord, whose kingdom they have diminished, who eat to the scandal of their brothers.
10.23: 10.23 All things are lawful for me. By the power of free will and the teaching of natural law. Not that all things, even unlawful ones, are lawful, but let us suppose that all things are lawful.
10.25: 10.25 Whatever is sold in the market. Because they are lawful, and yet they are not always to be used, he determines how it is lawful to eat or not to eat.
10.28: 10.28 For the sake of him. Because he who serves idols will thereby boast and be confirmed in error, and a bad example is given to the brothers.
10.29: 10.29 For why. As if: What need is there that I be thought to eat out of veneration? For I am judged not to differ from an idolater.
10.31: 10.31 Whether therefore you eat. Let not only your voice sound the praises of God, but let your works also agree with your voice. For when you have sung with the voice, you will sometimes be silent in life. But sing so that you are never silent. For if you cry out with your mouth and plan fraud in your mind, you have been silent from the praise of God, and what is graver, you have gone on to blasphemy. For when God is praised for your good work, you praise God; and when God is blasphemed for your evil work, you blaspheme God. If therefore you take what you eat and drink for the refreshment of the body and the repair of the limbs, giving thanks to him who gives you mortal and frail one these comforts of supply, your food and drink praise God. But if you exceed the measure due to nature by immoderate gluttony, and gorge yourself with wine, however many praises of God your tongue may sound, your life blasphemes.
10.32: 10.32 To the Church of God. As regards the weak, for whom offenses are made, when by their example they cling to things that are enemies of God.
10.33: 10.33 I please all. He who pleases men for the sake of truth, it is no longer he who pleases them but the truth. If a man pleases for his own sake, it is pride; this is what he said elsewhere: If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ, Galatians 1. But did he please his persecutors? He pleased every kind of men, because he gathered the Church of Christ, whether those already within or those to be brought into it.
11.1: 11.1 Imitators. There are degrees in the Church of greater and lesser, that the former may go before by example, the latter follow by imitation. But even those who go before, if they follow no one, will go astray: they therefore follow someone, that is Christ.
11.2: 11.2 I praise, etc. Here he begins to treat of head coverings, in which he rebukes them for not keeping his traditions: because some of them, men with covered head and some women with uncovered head, prayed or prophesied. Hence the Apostle is angry with them, because though he had been their Apostle, they were forgetful of his traditions, as if. Though I blame them on other points, I praise them in this: irony.
11.3: 11.3 Of the man, etc. By man may be understood here the spirit; not that Holy Spirit who remains unchangeable with the Father and the Son, and is given unchangeably to worthy souls, but the spirit of man, who as husband of the soul rules the animal affection as a wife. The head is Christ. Because the spirit of man is ruled by the wisdom of God, which is Christ: in whom as in the head are all spiritual senses, that is, the fullness of graces, from which this man receives, and by this the man is the head of the woman, that is, ruler of the animal nature, which is ruled by the spirit as a woman by a man. Praying. Because in other places she can be veiled, but she does not yet present herself to her judge and converse with him where she must profess her condition.
11.7: 11.7 Since the image. Image and likeness are taken for each other, but yet the likeness of the soul with God is properly in this: that it is uncircumscribed, that it is everywhere whole and at once. AUGUSTINE, book XII On the Trinity, chapters 7, 8, 9. Man is called the image of God, and according to the image: because he is not equal, etc., down to so that those who live badly may by speaking well cover their shame.
11.11: 11.11 Nevertheless. Although in the first creation the man is not from the woman but the other way, yet in the generation that follows this is not so. In the Lord. That is, in the operation of the Lord, in which neither is created without the other.
11.12: 11.12 And all things. After saying each point, in order to subject all to God as the one principle, he adds all things are from God, so that neither the woman may grieve at subjection nor the man be proud of exaltation.
11.13: 11.13 Judge for yourselves. Because the Corinthians had not kept his tradition (for which he is angry with them), he no longer persuades from the authority of tradition but from nature. Nature teaches us that if a man nourishes long hair, etc. Hair is a glory to a woman, because naturally she has it for a covering: for hair is a sign of a covering, so that the will of nature is added. And therefore the man is not naturally long-haired, because he is not to be veiled, and the law forbids a man to be long-haired.
11.14: 11.14 If a man, etc. The hair of Samuel and the prophets as a covering of the old law is laid aside in the revelation of the Gospel: hence when you pass over to Christ, the veil will be taken away.
11.17: 11.17 But this I command. Let it not be the skill of one deserting that is required, but let the authority of one commanding be heeded. Not praising. He begins to speak of the Lord's supper, in which they sinned much.
11.19: 11.19 There must be also heresies, etc. The Apostle does not wish or desire there to be heresies, but he says it because so it will be. And to what end this is useful he adds: that not only the reprobate (who say: I am of Paul) but also those who are approved may be made manifest. He says heresies for those who doubt the resurrection. There were divisions over spiritual gifts: and these to their own harm are of use to Catholics. For all the enemies of the Church, whether blinded by error or depraved by malice, are of use to the Church: for if they receive power to afflict bodily, they exercise her patience. But if by ill thinking they oppose, they exercise her wisdom.
11.20: 11.20 The Lord's supper. He calls the Lord's supper the receiving of the Eucharist, which they ought not to take after eating, or mix with their own meals, like those the Apostle rebukes, but fasting, in honor of so great a sacrament. For although after supper he gave his body and blood to his disciples, yet it is not to be calumniated against the whole Church that it is always received by those fasting. For the Savior, to commend more strongly the depth of this mystery, wished this last to be fixed in their hearts and memory. The order in which it should afterward be received he kept to be taught by the apostles, through whom he was going to set the churches in order.
11.21: 11.21 For each one, etc. He marks those who took back for themselves the gifts they offered at the altars for the sacrifice to be made, once it was done, and did not allow those who had none to share, but took them alone: so that they were even drunk from it, while others were hungry. AMBROSE. The gift offered becomes that of the whole people, etc., down to he repeats the form given by Christ in such a matter.
11.22: 11.22 The Church. The Church is the faithful, of whom it is said: That he might present to himself a glorious Church. Yet the Apostle testifies that even the house of prayer is called by this name, saying, Or the Church of God, etc. Do I praise you? Or distinguish thus: Do I praise you in this? Certainly I do not praise.
11.23: 11.23 For I received, etc. He shows that the mystery of the Eucharist, celebrated during a supper, is not a supper. For it is a spiritual medicine and a memorial of redemption, that we may attain greater things, because we were freed by the death of Christ. In eating and drinking we ought to be mindful of this, having attained the New Testament in it: because blood is the witness of the divine benefit, hence we receive it for the protection of body and soul: because the flesh of Christ is for the salvation of the body, the blood for our soul: and therefore the law foretold that blood is not to be eaten. In which night. In the night he suffered he came to the light of the resurrection.
11.24: 11.24 He broke. In the sacrament, that is, according to what seemed so and was believed by the faithful to be whole. He gave one to all, that they might remain in unity: but when he broke it, he showed his voluntary passion.
11.26: 11.26 As often as. He explains for what commemoration of Christ, namely his death. Until he comes. Because this will not be changed, as the sacraments of the Jews were.
11.27: 11.27 Unworthily. Not because someone eats it not for salvation is the body and blood he receives therefore less.
11.29: 11.29 Eats judgment to himself. The question is how this is, when the Lord says: He who eats me, the same will live because of me? But there are two ways of eating: one sacramental, in which both good and bad eat; the other spiritual, in which only the good. And this is not only to eat Christ and receive his body in the sacrament, but to remain in him and have him remaining in oneself. For he eats spiritually who remains in the unity of the Church (which the sacrament itself signifies). For he who is at odds with Christ neither eats the flesh of Christ nor drinks his blood, even if he receives the sacrament of so great a thing daily to judgment.
11.30: 11.30 Therefore among you. This happens for the correction of others.
11.32: 11.32 While we are judged, etc. For those who suffer, even their own punishment is sometimes a purification, as with the prophet Iddo, who ate though forbidden: who, alive, could be terrified or saddened over what he would not feel when dead. For it was said to him: Your body shall not be brought into the tomb of your fathers, III Kings 13. And by this the disobedience of the prophet could be punished, that his soul not be seized for the punishment of hell. We are chastised. In few is the amendment of all, so far as by fear of our punishment others are amended.
11.33: 11.33 Wait for one another. That the offering of many may be celebrated together, and it may be ministered to all.
12.1: 12.1 Concerning spiritual things. The Apostle begins to treat of the goods of the Holy Spirit, over whose greater ones some were proud, and the lesser ones envied and despised them, as if they were never to have them.
12.2: 12.2 You know. About to deliver spiritual things, he recalls what came first, that as they were then the image of idols, so now they may be the image of God.
12.3: 12.3 Therefore I make known. Because through each charism they gave men more glory than God, not knowing that this is ministered by the Holy Spirit; in all things he shows that praise and grace are God's, so that as then the image of the idol was all evil from man, so now all good things are believed to be from the Spirit of God. No one in the Spirit, etc. By thinking, speaking, doing. He says likewise in three ways, namely, in heart, mouth, and deed, anathema to Jesus, that is some separation from Jesus, that is any sin: as if: By the Spirit evil is abstained from. Except in the Holy Spirit. As if: To do well and every good is through the Holy Spirit, and therefore let not the greater despise the lesser, because he has nothing but from the Holy Spirit.
12.4: 12.4 Divisions. This is common to all: but the graces are divided, lest the lesser despair, lest the greater, hearing of graces, be proud.
12.6: 12.6 But the same God. He says this, lest the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit seem to work separate things, since he had put graces under the Spirit, and ministries under the Lord, and operations under God; referring all to one God, he adds: Because God works. All in all. He does not give all to one, but works all in all, that what one does not have in himself, he may have in another, and so charity and humility may remain.
12.7: 12.7 To each. The goods are divided, and are not given to anyone individually for merit, but for the usefulness of building up the Church. We too have received the Holy Spirit if we love the Church, if we are joined together by charity, if we rejoice in the Catholic name and faith. Let us believe, brothers, that as much as each one loves the Church of Christ, so much he has the Holy Spirit.
12.8: 12.8 Of wisdom. Wisdom is in the contemplation of eternal things. Knowledge in the action of temporal things. Hence in Job: Behold piety. That is, the worship of God is wisdom, which in Greek is theosebia. And what is this worship of him but love and knowledge of him? To abstain from evils is knowledge: and evils are in temporal things, in which one must move cautiously and prudently. He to whom wisdom is given is like the sun; he to whom knowledge, the moon in the night of the world; those to whom the rest are given are stars: because these are necessary in the night.
12.9: 12.9 To another faith. Faith too is among the gifts and gifts of God. Not charity alone, then, but charity with faith is from God to us.
12.10: 12.10 Of sermons. Sermons are allegorical utterances which appear in the prophets and the Gospels.
12.11: 12.11 One and the same Spirit. What he said above, that three work, here he names the Spirit: because since they are of one nature, what one does, the three do. One and the same, he says, lest there be thought to be as many as there are works: not that the Spirit works without the Father and the Son. For the working of the Trinity is inseparable. Dividing to each. Hence neither is this one to grieve nor that one to be proud. As he wills. Who alone knows what is fitting, and freely, not according to the merit of men.
12.12: 12.12 So also Christ. Christ is said to be head and body, because of the ineffable unity of head and members. One spirit will do all things in the members of the body of Christ, as one soul sees in the eye, hears in the ear, and in all the rest does all things.
12.13: 12.13 For indeed. He shows how the body of Christ is one, because we were all baptized, that is washed and led in one spirit to this, that we may be one body, that is of one mind through that one spirit, as the whole body of man is animated by one soul. And because we were all given to drink in receiving diverse gifts of the Holy Spirit, in one spirit: because he directs all gifts to make one. The person of none is to be despised or preferred, nor is the glory of God to be given to men: because one and the same works in all.
12.14: 12.14 For the body too. He shows by the likeness of the human body that the unity of the body of Christ, that is of the Church, has a variety of offices, and that this diversity does not remove unity: as the unity of the human body does not consist in singleness but in many members, that they may supply one another with what they owe.
12.17: 12.17 If the whole. As if to say: If in the Church all were of one office, how would the need of the body be met, whose government requires diverse things?
12.18: 12.18 Mark, each one of them as he willed. That nothing may be lacking to it: so also in the Church, various persons to whom he has assigned various gifts.
12.19: 12.19 But if all were one, not only would the multitude of senses perish, but the body also. So if in the Church all were of one office and dignity, neither the members nor the body would be distinguished.
12.21: 12.21 Or again the head to the feet. Dignity itself is contemptible without subjects. For it is an office by which dignity stands. A great emperor needs an army.
12.23: 12.23 Are unseemly. Far be it that there be any shame in the members of the saints: but they are called unseemly because they do not have that appearance of beauty which the visible ones have. Or on account of the law of the members which comes from sin; the unlawful use of the members is shameful, not the members themselves. Certain brothers are also understood, who, though honorable in poverty and dress, are sometimes of purer life. Or those are understood who in the Church are dishonorable through some sin, and are helped more abundantly by consolations and prayers, that they may become honorable.
12.24: 12.24 But the honorable. As if to say: So also for the brothers in whom the study of skill has adorned the honor of conduct, there is nothing for us to add. But God has tempered. Having removed what hinders, he puts what profits, namely harmony.
12.25: 12.25 But the same for one another. As if to say: Let the members be careful to aim at the same, that is, at that concern which is the same, that is, impartial, so that it is not less for another than for oneself.
12.26: 12.26 And if one suffers. This is not doubtful about the members of the body, because if the eye or foot is taken with some sickness, the whole body suffers with it. So it is fitting for us to suffer with our brothers if any adversity arises, and to rejoice if it turns out well.
12.27: 12.27 Of a member. Either of Christ, or of me, by whose preaching you were founded.
12.28: 12.28 And some indeed. Here he determines about the gifts of God, which are higher and which lower. For the Corinthians thought concerning these that the lesser was the greater and the greater the lesser. First. In dignity and time, apostles, preaching in the place of Christ and judges of all. Second, prophets. That is, those who reveal the mysteries of the Scriptures or things to come. Third, teachers. Those who give rules of living, or who instruct boys in letters. Kinds of tongues. CHRYSOSTOM. Behold, it is a gift of God to know many tongues. And note that he puts last that which they put first.
12.29: 12.29 Are all, etc. He who does not have these in himself, let him love them in others: and in them he already has these which he does not have in himself.
12.31: 12.31 A more excellent way. Charity, because it is a greater gift than all the aforesaid; hence at the end, to those who say, Lord, in your name we prophesied, cast out demons, did mighty works, the Lord will say: Depart from me, I do not know you, workers of iniquity, Matthew 7.
13.1: 13.1 If with tongues, etc. Here he proves that charity is more excellent: because the others without it do not avail, and it without them profits very much. But charity. Charity is the proper and unique fountain of goods, with which a stranger does not share. Which like oil cannot be pressed down to the bottom, but rises above; which if lacking, the rest are had in vain: if present, all are had. As sounding brass, etc. As brass resounds by some impulse and not of itself, so he who speaks with tongues does not speak of himself, who does not know what he says, but by the power of the spirit he brings forth what soothes the hearers.
13.2: 13.2 And if I have prophecy. As Balaam, and Caiaphas, and Saul. Should know mysteries. As Judas with the apostles, and the devil who (as Ezekiel says) knew the divine mysteries. Knowledge. As the scribes and Pharisees, hence: You have the key of knowledge, but you do not enter yourselves nor allow others to enter, Matthew 23. The wicked have these also, and they will confess in the judgment, where they will not dare to lie: to whom it will not be said: You did not have them, but I do not know you: because they had them without charity.
13.4: 13.4 Charity is patient, etc. These are the arms with which the soldier of Christ is armed. Of this armor he put first as chief weapons patience and kindness. ORIGEN. Patience bears evils inflicted by neighbors with equanimity, kindness lovingly bestows its goods on neighbors. Is not jealous. Because another's happiness does not sadden it. Is not puffed up. Because its own happiness does not lift it up.
13.5: 13.5 Does not seek, etc. It is not a lover of money.
13.7: 13.7 Believes all things. He does not say believes all men, because only God. Hopes all things. So it appeared in the fathers, that is in the people of Israel, who hoped to have what God promised. Endures all things. In the head, that is in Christ, who patiently awaited the glory of the resurrection and ascension.
13.8: 13.8 Charity. Again it is worthier in this that it ends neither in this age nor in the future, even if some of its works cease. Never falls away. If by believing and hoping we love what is not yet seen, how much more when it will be seen?
13.10: 13.10 Will be done away. It is the destruction of imperfection, when what is imperfect is fulfilled in full.
13.12: 13.12 Now. The images of truth are seen by faith. But then face to face. That is, the things themselves will be seen openly. Then I shall know. That is, I shall see the promises as he himself is, that is to be present with God, where Christ is. Or as I am foreknown to know what is now secret. Mirror. It is the soul: a mirror by whose power we know God in some way, but obscurely. Enigma. An enigma is not every allegory, but an obscure one. Hence as by mirror he signified an image, so by the name of enigma he understands a likeness, yet obscure and hard to grasp.
13.13: 13.13 Faith, hope, etc. With which knowledge and prophecy serve, and without which the life of no just man is perfect here. But the greatest of these is charity. Charity is that which faith and hope here cannot lack, but faith and hope can exist without charity.
14.2: 14.2 For he who speaks in a tongue, etc. This happened when the one speaking in a tongue did not understand himself, as if someone knew the pronunciation of some language and not its meaning
14.6: 14.6 But now. I said that he who prophesies is greater than he who speaks with a tongue. You can see in myself that a tongue does not profit, but prophecy does. But now. If I come to you now, when you are faithful, speaking in tongues, what shall I profit you? as if to say nothing; what then did a tongue profit then, when you were unbelievers? as if to say nothing. Or in revelation. That I may expound a revelation. Revelation is when some mysteries are shown through figures, as in the Apocalypse. Or in knowledge. That I may expound what pertains to knowing. These are what illumine the faith, as concerning the nature of the Godhead. Or in prophecy. That I may expound the Scriptures which treat of things to come. Or in doctrine. That I may expound the Scriptures which form morals.
14.7: 14.7 Yet things without, etc. By myself I showed that a tongue is of no avail without an interpreter. By myself I say, I showed, who am rational, yet I can show the same by inanimate things.
14.8: 14.8 For if an uncertain. Again by another comparison. For if uncertain, etc. The Jews used the trumpet in feasts and in wars with different sounds.
14.10: 14.10 And without voice. There are many tongues, but they have their own meanings of voices, that they may be understood.
14.11: 14.11 If then I do not know. And because others would not understand without an interpreter, I shall be a barbarian.
14.12: 14.12 So also you. Or under one distinction, so. And for this reason, that you not be barbarians, you too seek as I do that you may abound.
14.14: 14.14 My spirit prays. Spirit is called the power of the soul lower than the mind, where the likenesses of bodily things are impressed. Mind, the other higher power of the soul, as above. The spirit of Pharaoh was formed to see images; the mind of Joseph was enlightened to understand. Without fruit. So it is if someone speaks in an unknown tongue, or brings out signs of some things without understanding, as Latin men are wont to sing in Greek, delighted by the sound of the words, not knowing what they say.
14.15: 14.15 I will pray with the spirit. That is, I approve speaking so that the signs of things are formed in the spirit, and their meaning shines forth in the mind. Or, I will pray with the mouth and the mind.
14.16: 14.16 Amen. Note that this word amen is neither Greek nor Latin but Hebrew, and is interpreted true. And though it could be said, true, he did not say it, but amen. Neither the Greek nor the Latin interpreter dared do this, lest it become cheap when laid bare, but that it might have honor by the veil of secrecy.
14.18: 14.18 I thank God. He sets himself forth as an example, that they ought not to speak in tongues except for edification, like himself who knows them all.
14.20: 14.20 But in malice be children. Be removed from malice, like children, pursuing what profits, which is the perfection of sense.
14.21: 14.21 In the law. The reason why one ought not to seek tongues is that they are for a sign to unbelievers (which they themselves no longer are) and not for edification, which is now necessary for believers. In other tongues. Not about the sabbath, and new moons, and circumcision and such, but the New Testament. Or, not in revelation, of which they are unworthy, but in parables the Gospel is spoken to them. And even so they will not hear. This he foretold of those whom he foreknew would not believe, to whom on account of sins the truth is neither open nor pleasing.
14.22: 14.22 So then tongues are for a sign. That is, the words of God in an unknown and foreign tongue are obscure, so that they may not be seen by the unfaithful, that when they are heard, it may be a sign that it was done because of unfaithfulness, so that the hearers may not understand: this is certainly done to unbelievers, whose senses are covered, but to the faithful prophecy is fitting and not an unknown tongue.
14.23: 14.23 If then come together. Another reason is given here why they ought not to speak in tongues, as if to say, because tongues are for a sign, not for edification.
14.26: 14.26 What then. He now begins to determine how tongues are to be used; as if to say: Since these things come from the speaking of tongues; what is to be done about them? as if to say: Use tongues for edification, as the rest are to be done. Each, etc. So let no one excuse himself. Has a psalm. The praise of God, by song. Teaching. The spiritual sense by prudence.
14.27: 14.27 Or at most three. Not more than three, lest the one speaking in a tongue take up the day, and there be no place for the prophets discussing the Scriptures.
14.28: 14.28 Let him speak to himself. He speaks to himself who is pierced with compunction by what he says. And therefore to the honor of God, whom he praises or prays to.
14.29: 14.29 Two prophets. Because the speech of so many men suffices, and in the mouth of two or three every word stands.
14.30: 14.30 But if to another. It is given to the lesser, what is not to the greater.
14.33: 14.33 For God is not a God of dissension. But God would be a God of dissension if he compelled those whom he fills to speak at once. As in all, etc. Let women be silent, as I teach in all the churches.
14.35: 14.35 It is shameful. Because this is against ecclesiastical discipline.
14.37: 14.37 If anyone thinks he is a prophet. Which he certainly is not, if he does not acknowledge that it is so: for he who truly is a prophet acknowledges it so, and he who ignores these things will be ignored, that is, disapproved. The little ones who glory in the cross, even if they do not know what is most subtly discussed, nevertheless come to glory, because not one is lost of the little ones for whom Christ died. Let him acknowledge. In saying this he hints that the words of the epistles are difficult, since he bids that they be recognized by a prophet or a spiritual man.
14.38: 14.38 But if anyone does not know. But if anyone does not know these things, and does not wish to believe that they are commands of God, he will be ignored, as in the Gospel: I do not know you, that is, I do not know you to be mine, or among the predestined.
15.2: 15.2 By which also you are saved. If you hold fast that Gospel, that is the resurrection of the dead, by the reason by which I confirmed it to you, that is through the resurrection of Christ. Unless you believed in vain. That is, if you do not hold the resurrection of the dead. In vain is the faith that is not received in hope of the resurrection.
15.4: 15.4 He rose on the third day. And I said this according to the Scriptures. For Hosea says: After two days he will revive us, and on the third day we shall rise in his sight, Hosea 6. If he rose after being dead and buried, do not doubt that the dead and buried rise.
15.5: 15.5 He appeared to Cephas. Before the other men to whom he is read to have appeared in the Gospel, otherwise it would be contrary to what is read, that he appeared first to the women.
