15.8: 15.8 To one untimely born. He is called untimely born because born out of the lawful time, that is before he ought, or because, reborn later, he received the apostolate after Christ had already been taken up. Or like an untimely birth, because I am the least, either in time and calling, not in dignity, labor, and preaching. He truly said this out of humility, and proves it by saying: I am not worthy. Why then an Apostle? But by the grace of God. First by grace alone, when only bad merits preceded. But afterward by grace merits begin.
15.10: 15.10 More abundantly. This was more fulfilled, because he lived by the work of his hands, and did not do less for the Gospel. And lest the will without the grace of God be thought able to do anything, he adds: Not I, but the grace, etc
15.11: 15.11 And so you believed. He reproves them: because since this was the manifest faith among all the churches, they had nevertheless fallen away from it.
15.14: 15.14 But if Christ. Up to this point he has shown that Christ rose. Now through his resurrection he proves the resurrection of the dead. The false apostles denied that Christ truly suffered, or was buried, or rose, or came in the flesh.
15.15: 15.15 And we are found. These and other things are brought in so that the Corinthians, following the error of the false apostles, may blush, as these absurd things follow from it, which he himself also condemns. So that they may not remain in this error, he says: I found, etc. Against God. Not less, but perhaps with greater crime falsehood is praised in God than truth is blamed.
15.17: 15.17 But if Christ is not, etc. If Christ has not risen; Christ is held in death. And if in death, then also in sin, which is the cause of death. And if he is held in sin, he could not remit your sins. And so you are still in your sins, which you believed were remitted to you, and so your faith is vain.
15.21: 15.21 For since by a man. Behold the first fruits, man and man, man to life, man to death, but that one only man, this one God and man.
15.22: 15.22 And as. By as, likeness and cause are noted, because as from the corruption of Adam to death, so from the spirit of Christ to life.
15.23: 15.23 Each. He explains the orders, as of a sure thing: and the times when it has been done, and when it will be, that the dead rise. Then those who are. Another reading: Then those who are Christ's at his coming, namely, will rise. So those who believe in Christ and are less worthy than he will rise later in time and lesser in dignity. And who are Christ's he explains, adding: Who believed in his coming, etc.
15.24: 15.24 Then the end. He puts this to commend the resurrection, which being fulfilled will be the end of the world and the consummation of all. When he shall have abolished. While the world lasts, angels rule over angels, demons over demons, men over men: for the benefit of the living, or for deception. But when men are gathered among angels and men, all rule will cease, there will not be that dissension between those who preside and those who are subject. Then it will be known to all that none of these, earthly or heavenly, had anything of themselves, but from him from whom are all things.
15.25: 15.25 For he must reign. The sense is: His kingdom must meanwhile be made manifest, until all enemies confess that he reigns: by saying until he excludes a greater manifestation, not a longer continuance of the kingdom. Hence elsewhere: Our eyes are on the Lord our God, until he have mercy, etc. Not that then they turn away, but that they seek nothing further.
15.26: 15.26 And the last. Among other things it is evident that Christ also has the power of raising when he adds: The last enemy to be destroyed is death. Now Christ reigns, and then he will reign: but last, that is after all, death will be destroyed, because men will no longer be dissolved as heretics suppose. Last. Because there will be nothing left to destroy; after this mortal puts on immortality. Enemy. Whom we are enemies to, or itself to us. Again a commendation of the resurrection.
15.27: 15.27 Except him who put all things under him. Who, as he is from none, so by no reason can he be subject to any: for he himself is the beginning of all. That God may be all. Because when every creature will say that Christ is its head, and the head of Christ is God, not only in all, that is in the confession of all, will God be one, but every creature will also confess that he is the one from whom are all things.
15.28: 15.28 That God may be. He is the end which above, so often concluding, he put: afterward he explains member by member what the future consummation will be. All. Which can be desired. In all, his members: because the reward of virtue will be he himself who gave the virtue, because God will be that from which they are satisfied.
15.29: 15.29 For the dead. That is, for sins to be destroyed. Or, to make themselves dead to the likeness of the death of Christ, what will they do when they are not to have life? If altogether, etc. So that Christ has not even risen? Why are they baptized when sins are not forgiven, if Christ has not risen?
15.31: 15.31 For your. Or: By your glory. Behold the Apostle swears that we may know that to swear truly is not sin, but we are not therefore to swear in doubtful matters; and it is safer not to swear than by the habit of swearing to perjure oneself. But to swear falsely is a most grave sin. An oath is not against the precept: which is not from the evil of the one who swears, but of the unbelieving or weak, who does not otherwise believe.
15.32: 15.32 If according to man. That is, acting rationally, because it is of man to believe, not to die as a beast, I fought, that is I disputed. Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. This for those who, as if nothing is to be after death, care only for the belly like cattle, saying: Who has come from there? I have not heard the voice of anyone coming from there. To whom it is said: Fool, if your father rose, would you believe? The Lord of all rose, and you do not believe. He who wished to die and rise, that all might believe in one, that we might not be deceived by many. You would believe a father about to die again, and you do not believe him now immortal, who finally has testimony in heaven, testimony on earth, testimony from angels, testimony from those below.
15.33: 15.33 Do not be deceived, etc., by the false apostles; who seek a wound from medicine and try to twist a chain from the Scriptures, from which they may cast a noose of death. They corrupt good morals, etc. THEODORET. Here he called good those who are light, who are easily deceived.
15.34: 15.34 Awake. Do not this, but awake from the body; and so you will be just; and after: Do not sin by consenting to them, because they do not know God.
15.35: 15.35 But someone will say. Up to now he has proved by reasons the resurrection of the dead, now he shows that it can come about by the very nature of things; as if to say by these it is proved: but still some depraved person could speak as though the resurrection of the dead could not come about by nature: And if they rise: with what body, as if to say: It cannot be other than now, that is passible and mortal. The Apostle answers: Fool, that is you who do not attend to what you see daily in the grain.
15.36: 15.36 You fool: what you sow. So the dead will be able to live, and in a better body: so that what you sow rises better.
15.38: 15.38 But God gives. As therefore the bare grain is sown, and by the will of God rises as if clothed, having with it many increases, so the dead by the power of God will be able to live and rise in a better body. To each of the seeds. So also he will restore to us our old bodies, as Job says: Whom I myself shall see, and not another. But there will be a difference in glory and dignity, though they are of the same nature. As not all flesh is of the same dignity, though from the same elements, and this is what he says:
15.39: 15.39 And the same flesh. All flesh is body, but not the other way: as wood.
15.40: 15.40 Heavenly. The bodies of the risen are heavenly; earthly before they die, because from Adam. And because Christ is heavenly, bodies are called heavenly from him, and are no longer called flesh. But from Adam, because he is earthly, earthly bodies are named.
15.41: 15.41 For star differs from star, etc. In my Father's house are many mansions, though the same denarius, that is eternal life, to all. For there is one blessedness which the just receive; but unequal the quality of reward. Though the risen are of unequal brightness, yet God is all in all, because God is charity, and by charity it will be that what each has is common to all.
15.42: 15.42 It is sown. That is, although man from conception until dissolution is in corruption and afterward teems with worms, yet he will rise in incorruption.
15.44: 15.44 A natural body. That is, which has nothing from the soul except that it is given sense by it, as animals. It will rise spiritual. Passing into the nature of spirit, that is having certain spiritual things, because agile, light, not needing food. When he said the body would pass to incorruption, he makes mention of corruption to show the greater dignity of the resurrection. If there is a body. Truly a spiritual body will rise, because if it is now natural, that is it is so, it will at some time be spiritual. For as we are natural because our father was made carnal into a living soul: so we shall be spiritual in the resurrection: because our Father became spiritual in his resurrection into a life-giving spirit.
15.45: 15.45 Man. The whole human race is in a manner those two men, first and second: from the one born, from this reborn. Christ is called Adam, because from the same matter; last, because after him no other man succeeds who is head or author of the human body. But not. He said our bodies will be spiritual; but lest anyone doubt whether the natural can become spiritual, he proves it by the likeness of Christ; as if to say, he was made a life-giving spirit. But that was not first in him which is spiritual, but that which is natural, then the spiritual. So also it can be with us.
15.47: 15.47 The first man. Truly first into a living soul; because he was formed from the dust of the earth natural and passible by nature. The second man, because from heaven, that is because the divine nature was united to the human, therefore heavenly, that is spiritual in the resurrection; and because the first father was earthly, all such are earthly. Heavenly. Christ is said to be so, because he was conceived and born not by human custom but by divine will.
15.50: 15.50 But this I say. The Jews believed in a future resurrection, but after the manner of this life, that they should marry and beget: hence some could not answer the Sadducees about the woman with seven husbands, for they were thinking carnally of the resurrection: but the Apostle removes this, saying: That flesh. By flesh and blood he signifies belly and lust, that is the works of the flesh (which will not be there). Nor will corruption inherit incorruption. Lest you think it is said according to the substance of the flesh, he made it clear. He therefore said that flesh will not possess the kingdom of God: because the corruption of mortality, which here is shown by the name of flesh, will not possess incorruptibility.
15.51: 15.51 We shall indeed all. Or (according to Jerome, who asserts that the living found will not die, writing to Marcella) all the dead will rise, and not all the living found will be changed, but the saints only.
15.52: 15.52 In the last. That is in the last sign, which will be given that these things be fulfilled. This trumpet is the cry of which it is said: At midnight a cry was made: behold the bridegroom comes. By the name of trumpet some evident and illustrious sign is meant, which is elsewhere called the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, and in the Gospel the voice which the dead who are in the tombs will hear and come forth, etc. We shall be changed. He explains how this will be, or what the change is.
15.54: 15.54 Is swallowed up. That is destroyed in the victory of Christ; or in that it went beyond the manner of conquering by attacking Christ; or death is delight in sin with consent, which is conquered in that the servants of God will conquer the desires of their flesh.
15.55: 15.55 O death, where is your victory? These are the words of the prophet, or of the Apostle rejoicing and mocking death in the person of the risen, that the resurrection may be more certain: as if to say: You conquered in the dying, you are conquered in the rising. Your victory by which you had swallowed the bodies of the dying was temporal: that by which you are swallowed up in the bodies of the risen will stand eternal.
16.1: 16.1 Concerning the collections. After other matters, he briefly admonishes about the collections to be made for the saints who were in Jerusalem. This is not against the saying: Do not think about tomorrow. For it is not to think about tomorrow if one thinks of these things in a human way: but if someone serves God for the sake of these things, so that in his works he looks not to the kingdom of God but to the acquiring of these things. So you also. AMBROSE. The Apostle commands that all the people come together on the Lord's day, etc., down to nor is it heavy, and much is found.
16.2: 16.2 Through, etc. That is, on the Lord's day. Because among the Jews this day, which we Christians call the Lord's day, is called one day of the sabbath, or one of the sabbaths, or the first of the sabbath.
16.6: 16.6 I shall stay with you, or even winter, etc. There, like a physician, he made a stay where many were sick.
16.15: 16.15 Now I beseech you, brothers, you know the house of Stephanas and Fortunatus, etc. The order of this letter looks to and depends upon that point, that you also be subject.
16.18: 16.18 My spirit and yours, etc. Mine, in joy: yours, in charity.
